processing_steps.temperature: initial rolling temperature approximately 1050 °C, finishing rolling temperature approximately 950 °C

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Hot rolled from 80 to 12 mm thickness in eight passes.

structures.overall_structure: Micro-laminated microstructure consisting of δ-ferrite bands and tempered martensite lamellar, maintained after intercritical quenching-annealing. After annealing, a large number of fine austenite grains (reverted austenite plus retained austenite) are widely distributed in the tempered martensite region. At the annealing temperature of 620 °C, carbides (considered to be cementite) precipitate and are widely distributed in the tempered martensite.

microstructure_list.region: tempered martensite region (fine grains widely distributed)

phases_present.morphology: fine austenite grains widely distributed in tempered martensite region

grain_structure.grain_size_distribution: Austenite grain-size distribution of QA specimens decreases monotonically with size; around 90 % of grains were less than 4.8 μm, most austenite grains <2.0 μm.

phases_present.morphology: fine carbides widely distributed in tempered martensite

defect_interactions.interaction_type: stress concentration / crack initiation at δ-ferrite / γ-α interface; second cracks
defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: Due to the hardness difference between δ-ferrite and tempered martensite, stress concentration readily occurred at their interfaces, inducing crack initiation. Once formed, cracks were captured by δ-ferrite and propagated into and along the δ-ferrite band, forming second cracks like deep valleys (Fig. 6); crack propagation into soft δ-ferrite could be blunted (high resistance).

For QA-620, the precipitation of carbides strongly retarded dislocation gliding, greatly enhancing yield and tensile strength; the WHR of QA-620 was apparently higher than other QA specimens at true strain 0.01–0.1.

interfaces.slip_behavior: Ductile deformation started in the soft phase (ferrite, austenite); carbides in QA-620 strongly retarded dislocation gliding, raising yield and tensile strength, while decreased alloy-element content in the matrix reduced lattice distortion of tempered martensite, raising deformability. TRIP effect (and TWIP effect) occurred during deformation.
interfaces.phase_evolution: Water-quenched plate (IQ-1050) annealed at 620 °C for 1 h: retained austenite fraction increased and reverted austenite nucleated and grew at martensite lath gaps with C and Mn diffusing into austenite and Al into martensite/ferrite; recovery decreased GND density. At 620 °C, carbides precipitate (below the ~617 °C A1 cementite precipitation point).
interfaces.interface_notes: Cracks propagated and were arrested along the δ-ferrite bands; second cracks observed in tensile fracture of QA specimens.

measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: rod-shaped sample size of M10*60 mm with gauge length of 25 mm
measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Tensile axis parallel to the rolling direction of the hot-rolled plate. Annealing temperature 620 °C for 1 h (QA-620).

tensile_properties.stress_strain_curves: Engineering stress-strain curve of QA-620 plotted in Fig. 5(a) (QA curves plateau ~700–850 MPa with far larger elongation; engineering strain up to 70 %).
strain_hardening_rate: WHR of QA-620 was apparently higher than that of other QA specimens at true strain 0.01–0.1, attributed to precipitated carbides intensely retarding dislocation gliding

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Austenite volume fraction measured by EBSD and XRD (before tensile test).

comparative_performance.comparison_metric: Yield strength and tensile strength of QA-620 were much higher than those of the other QA specimens (QA-680, QA-740, QA-800), principally associated with precipitated carbides in QA-620; all QA specimens exhibited PSE > 30 GPa% and low yield-to-tensile ratio. The experimental steel after QA treatment could substitute for TRIP 590T/400Y from SAE J2745-2007 standard (also stated as TRIP 580T/400Y).

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: equilibrium phase fraction and composition vs temperature

computational_details.validation_against_experiment: Used to select quenching temperature (1050 °C, ferrite + austenite dual-phase region) and annealing temperatures (620, 680, 740, 800 °C); cementite precipitation point ~617 °C justified the 620–800 °C annealing window.

computational_details.simulation_method: geometrically necessary dislocation (GND) density calculation from EBSD KAM data
computational_details.software_used: HKL Channel5 and Python (EBSD data analysis)
computational_details.boundary_and_initial_conditions: Burger's vector b = 2.887 Å for BCC and 2.563 Å for FCC (measured by XRD); EBSD step size μ = 150 nm

analytical_models.equation_role: ρGND = 2 KAM_ave / (μ b), computing GND density from average local misorientation
analytical_models.model_note: KAM_ave computed by Eq. 2 as the exponential of the mean of ln KAM_i.

computational_details.simulation_method: stacking fault energy (SFE) estimation from XRD Rietveld refinement
computational_details.boundary_and_initial_conditions: Parameters from Rietveld refinement of XRD profiles; ε²₅₀ root-mean-square microstrain in <111> direction averaged over 50 Å distance
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: TWIP effect inferred for QA specimens since SFE between 20 and 40 mJ/m².

analytical_models.model_note: A = Zener elastic anisotropy; G<111> = shear modulus in <111>; a0 = lattice constant.

computational_details.boundary_and_initial_conditions: V0 and Vε = austenite volume fraction before and after tensile tests; ε = corresponding true strain after tensile tests
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: k value inversely related to SFE; QA-620 k = 1.24 (higher k means lower austenitic stability).

analytical_models.equation_role: Vε = V0 exp(−kε), where k is the austenitic mechanical stability constant
analytical_models.model_note: Higher k value means lower austenitic stability.

unmapped_findings: The 620 °C annealed specimen (QA-620) is the only QA condition in which carbides (Cm, considered to be cementite) precipitated and were widely distributed in the tempered martensite, because 620 °C is below the A1 cementite precipitation temperature (~617 °C).

For QA-620, the precipitation of carbides strongly retarded dislocation gliding to greatly enhance yield and tensile strength, while the decrease of alloy element content in the matrix reduced the lattice distortion of tempered martensite to rise the deformability of the steel (positive to ductility).

For QA-620, the precipitation of carbides and the lower annealing temperature reduced the SFE of the austenite in comparison with QA-680; its austenitic stability was therefore lower than that of the 680 °C annealed specimen.

In the tensile fracture of QA-620, significantly smaller micro-dimples than other specimens were observed; river pattern (propagation of cleavage cracks) was stopped by ductile fracture areas (dimples). Cleavage and quasi-cleavage features were associated with δ-ferrite.
QA-620 austenitic mechanical stability constant k = 1.24 (Fig. 9c), intermediate between QA-680 (0.56) and QA-740 (1.47)/QA-800 (1.50), indicating a moderate TRIP effect.

More austenite underwent TRIP effect in QA-620 than in QA-680, which neutralized the improvement of ductility of QA-680 due to its lower GND density; hence total elongation of QA-620 (~44.0 %) was almost the same as that of QA-680 (~45.6 %).

For all QA specimens including QA-620, the austenite grain-size distribution decreased monotonically with increasing size, with around 90 % of grains smaller than 4.8 μm (most austenite grains <2.0 μm).

All annealed specimens including QA-620 exhibited three-stage work hardening characteristics, in which stages II and III resulted from the competition between dislocation gliding and TRIP effect combined with TWIP effect, according to their SFEs (between 20 and 40 mJ/m²).
